en: May the auspicious characteristic of the matted locks be present; salutations to the illustrious Lord of the Gaṇas.
May there be prosperity!
That brahmin who desires to speak of the *jaṭā* is the best among those who know the Vedas;
his fame shall increase, and he enjoys the fruit of the Vedas. 1.
Having proceeded through two words, skipping over them again and again with a continuous flow, one should employ them joined according to their natural phonetic form; that is considered *jaṭā*.
This is declared to be the *prakṛti* (base form) of the *saṃhitā* of the word-order.

Understand that this is the nature of the *jaṭā* (interwoven recitation) as it exists eternally. When the *jaṭā* is about to be performed, the tremors, joints, tones, and so forth should be extracted and applied skillfully; that has been declared by the experts.
One who knows the Prātiśākhya and other treatises, who is proficient in all the Śikṣās,

and who is endowed with the power of intelligence, is fit to explain the *jaṭā* [arrangement], including elision (*lopa*), non-elision (*alopa*), augmentation (*ūṣmatva*), substitution (*ādeśa*), and addition (*āgama*).

Just as it has been declared in the *Saṃhitā*, so indeed it is in the *Jaṭā*. In the *Āruṣa* [system], for one who possesses [the mantra], there is no [defect] due to the dual arrangement of the letter *ra*; likewise, such a state exists even in the *Mānuṣa* [system], but not from any other source.
Just as the rule for those vowels that are to be held (*pragṛhya*) is prescribed according to their recitation, so too has the rule for them when pronounced out of order been derived from grammar;
however, regarding the phoneme in *saṃhitā* which is prescribed to have the status of being held (*pragraha*), [the following applies].
That very *cakra* proceeds toward this state of *jaṭā*;
for the sake of the two steps, even when one is absent,
the sequence there should be understood as being like the *saṃhitā*, and likewise should *jaṭā* be understood by those who hold this view.
For all those who possess short [syllables], there is shortness in the first half-verse;
however, at the beginning and end of the second half-verse, it should always be long.
As for the sequence, it follows the recitation; indeed, even for one who is not afflicted, there may be both direct and reverse order.
Otherwise, the established rule is that these two [words] must indeed be preceded by a word:
"svadhā māpā asi paro jyā āpūṣā prabudhniyā aminantam";
for these seven do not attain their proper euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) unless they are followed by a word of a seer (*ārṣa*). 12–13.
When [the suffix] *uṇ* follows a conjunct consonant (*pṛkta*), there should be a long vowel; however, when it follows a single phoneme (*varṇa*), or rather, when there is the substitution of *ū*,
then for that reason, even from the *saṃhitā* [text],
the initial *ca* and so forth are elided, and there is the elision of *m* when followed by *kṣ*.
In that case, the substitution of *bhū* for every preceding *as* is not desired.
However, regarding the three-fold sequence (*trikrama*) which will be explained [later], first there is the sequence of three words;
then, by means of the middle and the last [words] among them, there is no distinction beyond that.
In the *Trikrama*, however, there is only the ascent (*rohaṇa*) of three steps, and likewise their descent (*ārohaṇa*); subsequently, that which is preceded by the prefix *ā-* is desired.
Now, regarding the *Kampa*:
The *nitya*, the *abhinihita*, the *kṣaipra*, and the *praśliṣṭa*—

these *svāra* [svarita] vowels tremble when followed by an acute (*udātta*) or a circumflex (*svarita*) vowel. Furthermore, when a circumflex vowel follows, the upper half of that circumflex [is affected].
One should utter that [vowel] long with a tremor when it follows a low-pitched syllable;
likewise, there are tremors at the end of a word. At the end, the remaining [syllables] may be either udātta or svarita, according to the established rule, with their anuśvāras suppressed. 19–20.

One should make what is not long appear as long; that which is employed with a discordant tone, with tremors, or with excessive high-pitched singing, as well as shortening and stretching, should be done.
However, one should tremble in the middle, and both sides should be equal.
One should cause the *saraṅga* to tremble with a trembling, just as a charioteer [makes his horses tremble]; this is the illustration (22).
The *svārās*, *kampas*, and *raṅgas*, whatever their natural duration may be, increase when they are being proclaimed, even when the speaker is using a rapid instrument (23).
An anusvāra that is to be grasped as svarita, as well as the dhara-lavas,
are considered to be grasped as svarita when joined with a following vowel.
A short vowel preceding [the svarita] is accented, while the long vowel at the end of the portion has the two [svarita and udātta] following it.
Only the *nāda* and the *anusvāra* are accented like the preceding high-pitched vowel (udātta).
Where there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*), that [vowel] is accented as high-pitched by the wise; but when a conjunction follows, the final long vowel becomes circumflex (*svarita*).

Neither *pluta* nor *pragraha* [elision] is applied as a sandhi operation; rather, at that time, there is either a single *mātrā* or an excess of *mātrās*. Again, [the word] *carpitaścakaḥ* ends with *suvarakarho*.

The sequence of words beginning with *ajīgarit* is to be recited together with the letter *ra*. The rule concerning *hvāra*, *bhāra*, and so forth is applicable; however, a long vowel followed by *na* or *kā* does not apply when a *ra* occurs in the middle of a verse-quarter (*pāda*).
If, however, there were elision [of the vowel] after this [consonant], these two [rules] would not apply elsewhere;

for in the case of *anvi*, when there is a consonant as the cause for the elision of the letter *a* in the formation of *jaṭā*, there would be no elision at all, just as in the case of *saṃhitamantarā*.
It is traditionally taught that the *madhyasthanāsikya* (the nasal sound situated between the vowels) is not in conflict with the rule;

therefore, let those who know the dharma of the social classes perform their duties. In the *saṃhitā*, words should remain in their original form (*prakṛti*), and indeed, the words as they were spoken should not be altered.
In the *jaṭā* arrangement, the operation should be as if there were a *saṃdhi*; in the *saṃhitā* arrangement, it is not as if there were a *saṃdhi*.
(32) Even for an uncombined (*apṛkta*) *u*-vowel, both a lengthening and an augment may occur;
therefore, in these two cases, there would be a long vowel, whereas elsewhere there would be only an augment. (33)
However, that long vowel which occurs in the *saṃhitā* when followed by consonants should become short at the time of the *padapāṭha*; it is likewise in the *jaṭāpāṭha*.
[This applies] according to the rule "after a prefix" (*upasargāt*) before a verbal root (*dhātu*).
According to Vāsupya Āpiśali: "as in the *saṃhitā* between [words]. This means "without the *saṃhitā*.
In the preceding utterance of *anvi*, there would not be the *t* of the *jaṭā* for the vowel *ā*.

The state of being the fourth (turīyatva) is prescribed for the very word that possesses the function [of denoting Brahman], while its state of being the second among the Brāhmaṇas is stated again by way of the context;
thus ends the definition of the *jaṭā*.
